A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CYBERTEAM benchmark. Their main text, tables, figures, equations and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM and cybersecurity-agent evaluations, individual-task results, noise-robustness experiments and runtime measurements.

after.justification: v3 reports benchmark evaluations and adds human acceptance judgments, module ablations, token-consumption measurements and non-LLM comparisons.

M1.justification: Appendix B makes limited changes to prescribed prompts: SUM requests 3–5 sentences instead of 3–4, and NER explicitly requests additional entity categories such as techniques and target assets. The dependency-chain architecture and nine modules persist. Expanded retrieval, validation and retry descriptions do not establish that these components were newly introduced.

E1.justification: Tables 1–2 retain 452,293 instances, 30 tasks and 23 sources across the same four threat-hunting stages. New evaluations examine retained tasks; expanded collection documentation and discussion of unseen threats do not establish additional evaluated domains or scenarios.

E2.justification: v3 adds actual non-LLM comparisons in Table 9: TF-IDF for malware identification, regex extraction for signature matching, cosine similarity for temporal matching and LSTM classifiers for three classification tasks. It also distinguishes CYBERTEAM (LLM) and CYBERTEAM (Full). The existing ICL5, ICL10, CoT and ToT comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The reported model lineup replaces GPT-4o, GPT-o4-mini and Gemini-2.5 with Grok-4.1, GPT-5.1 and Gemini-3. New protocols include binary analyst acceptance judgments, controlled single-module removals and generated-token accounting. Existing task metrics, noise perturbations and Table 4 query settings remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's noise tests, runtime analysis and case studies, v3 adds NER/SPA/SUM/RAG removal experiments in Appendix E.4, token-efficiency analysis in E.5 and qualitative NER/RAG failure analysis in Appendix F. These examine component contributions, computational tradeoffs and downstream error propagation.

E5.justification: Table 3 changes from point estimates to values with ± terms throughout. New Table 6 explicitly reports acceptance-rate means and standard deviations across three human evaluators. However, v3 does not define Table 3's ± terms or supply corresponding run counts or seeds, so additional repeated experiments cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Tables 6–9 add extensive human, ablation, token-cost and classical-baseline results. Table 3 also changes model-linked entries: standardized playbook scores of 84.6/91.4 for GPT-4o/o4-mini become 85.9/92.7 for Grok/GPT-5.1, which is not a same-model gain. Table 5 retains its numerical values while changing model attribution; several figures likewise identify different models.

T1.justification: The task/module formulation, CVSS equations, span metrics and Appendix C metric definitions remain mathematically unchanged. v3 adds implementation explanations, without new theorems, proofs or substantive derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same central claims: a broad blue-team benchmark, dependency-aware standardized reasoning using nine modules, and advantages over open-ended prompting. The revised conclusion preserves this scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of module importance, analyst disagreement and token-efficiency tradeoffs. Appendix F newly discusses adversarial evaluation boundaries and explains how unusual entity formats and irrelevant retrieval can propagate errors. These extend the existing dataset-generalizability limitation rather than merely relocating it.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.2 documents normalization, validation, human checking and deduplication, including a MinHash/Jaccard threshold of 0.85. Appendix B substantially expands schemas, prompts, retrieval infrastructure and fault-handling details. These are primarily new disclosures; hardware and query settings persist. Conversely, v1's explicit project code-access link is absent from v3.

R1.justification: v3 adds Hasanov et al.'s cybersecurity review and removes distinct references including HackSynth, Hossen et al. and Sawant et al. Many other citation differences are publication updates or deduplication. The positioning around interdependent blue-team workflows remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Appendix B extensively expands and reorganizes existing explanations into implementation, fault-tolerance and structured prompt descriptions. The introduction, individual-task discussion and conclusion are edited, and v3 adds an appendix contents page and experiment roadmap. The former LLM-usage disclosure disappears, while Appendix F becomes a discussion section.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column presentation with redesigned headings, running headers and callout styling. Existing figures and tables are resized and relocated, model labels change, Table 3 accommodates uncertainty notation, and four new experimental tables are added. Existing workflow diagrams largely retain their content.

improvement.justification: Table 7's controlled ablations strengthen support for module-importance claims that v1 left untested, while Appendices A.2/B make benchmark construction and implementation more inspectable. However, new validation remains incompletely documented, Table 3's uncertainty is undefined, and the code-access link disappears. v3 also incorrectly attributes scores above 90% and 92% to Grok, whose corresponding Table 3 scores are 85.9% and 81.6%. These shortcomings limit the net improvement.
